text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
One of the most attractive of flowers, the FUCHSIA, is named after German botanist LEONARD FUCHS who was born on this day in 1501.

BENJAMIN FRANKLIN was born in 1706. He helped draft the "Declaration of Independence", but is better known for inventing bi-focal glasses, the rocking chair, the lightning conductor and the water-powered harmonica.
Australian author and illustrator CECILIA MAY GIBBS was born in 1877. She lived in a Sydney home she called NUTCOTE and brought us the bushland characters SNUGGLEPOT and CUDDLEPIE.
The British novelist NEVILLE SHUTE, who settled in Australia where he set his most famous book "A TOWN LIKE ALICE", was born in 1899.
The American gangster known as "SCARFACE", AL CAPONE, was also born in 1899.
Australian consumer affairs expert SYDNEY EINFELD, who gained great respect as a NSW Cabinet Minister, was born on this day in 1909.
Australian industrialist and soccer administrator Sir ARTHUR GEORGE was born in 1915.
Cricketer CLYDE WALCOTT from Barbados was born in 1926. He once, with FRANK WORRELL, hit an unbroken stand of 544 against Trinidad.
The three-time world heavyweight boxing champion MUHAMMAD ALI was born on this day in 1942.
Prominent Australian journalist and magazine editor ITA CLARE BUTTROSE was also born on this day in 1942.

British singer/songwriter PAUL YOUNG was born in 1956. After an early career setback by losing his voice PAUL went on to find popularity as a solo performer. He had a hit immediately with "Wherever I Lay My Hat (That's My Home)"(1983). Other hits included "Come Back And Stay"(1983), "Love Of The Common People" (1983), "Everything Must Change" (1984) and "Every Time You Go Away" (1985).

'Bangles' singer/songwriter SUSANNA HOFFS was born in 1961. The group first called themselves the 'Bangs' in 1981. In mid-1982 they changed to the 'Bangles'. They had their first hit with "Manic Monday" in 1986, which was written by PRINCE. Other hits included "Walk Like An Egyptian" (1986), "Hazy Shade Of Winter" (1987) and "Eternal Flame" (1989).
**EVENTS**
1773 : Captain COOK's "RESOLUTION" crossed the Antarctic
Circle, the first ship ever to do so.
1874 : Famous Siamese twins CHANG and ENG (which means
"left" and "right" in Thailand) died within 3 hours of each other, at the age of 62.
1912 : British polar explorer Captain ROBERT FALCON SCOTT
and his team reached the South Pole, only to discover a Norwegian team had beaten them there by just one month.
1929 : POPEYE THE SAILOR made his first appearance in the
comic strip "THIMBLE THEATRE".
1933 : The Australian Cricket Board complained to the MCC

(Marylebone Cricket Club) at Lords over the "bodyline" bowling tactics of DOUGLAS JARDINE's touring Englishside. The English bowlers, led by HAROLD LARWOOD, had injured several Australian players during the 3rd Test in Adelaide. It was feared spectators would riot when the popular BERT OLDFIELD was carried from the field, unconscious.
1934 : A poor man called POHL found a 500-carat diamond
near Pretoria in South Africa.
1951 : A group of striking Aborigines marched on Darwin.

The Northern Territory Aborigines went on strike demanding equal rights with white workers and a weekly wage of seven pounds. The marchers were dispersed by police. The Aboriginal wage for government work was two pounds a week or one pound, plus keep, for private employment.
1966 : A B-52 carrying four hydrogen bombs collided with
a refuelling tanker, killing 8 people and releasing the weapons.
1972 : Australia's Aboriginal tennis star EVONNE
GOOLAGONG, who was awarded an MBE on New Year's Day, was named Australian of the Year.
1977 : United States convicted murderer GARY GILMORE

became the first prisoner to be executed in America for ten years. "Let's do it" were his last words as he was led out to face the firing squad at the Utah State Prison. GILMORE was found guilty of murdering two students at the Brigham Young University in 1976 and had called for his own execution. Despite this his sentence became the something of a test case and was the subject of protest. An earlier stay of execution was lifted by the US Court of Appeals.
1988 : Nicaraguan SANDINISTA leader DANIEL ORTEGA offered
a ceasefire to the CONTRA rebels fighting the Government.
1989 : A self-styled "RAMBO" opened fire in a school
playground in Stockton, California, killing five children and injuring 30 others.
1994 : An earthquake measuring 6.6 on the Richter scale
struck Los Angeles, killing 61 people and causing extensive damage.
1994 : Contender for the US Olympic ice-skating team

TONYA HARDING denied any involvement in the bashing of rival American ice-skater NANCY KERRIGAN. TONYA'S ex-husband JEFF GILLOOLY was arrested over the incident and convicted. TONYA later admitted her guilt in the plan to cripple KERRIGAN. KERRIGAN, who turned a medal winning performance at the Winter Olympics at Lillehammer, also won world sympathy. HARDING suffered from public scorn and not surprisingly performed poorly at the games.
1995 : More than 6,000 people were killed after a strong
earthquake ripped through central Japan. Measuring 7.2 on the Richter scale, the earthquake centred around the port of Kobe was the biggest quake to hit Japan in half a century.
